title: System Design
summary: Designing large-scale systems that stay fast, available and correct as load grows.
hook: Every design is a trade: you buy speed, scale or safety with complexity and money.

cards.q: Name the first five questions you ask in a system design interview.
cards.a: Who uses it and how; scale (users, QPS, data size); read/write ratio; latency and consistency needs; what's out of scope.

cards.q: What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?
cards.a: Functional: what it does (post, follow). Non-functional: how well (latency, availability, durability).

children.title: Fundamentals
children.summary: Latency, throughput, availability and the tradeoffs that shape every design.
children.hook: A highway: latency is the drive time, throughput is cars per hour.

cards.q: Define latency vs throughput.
cards.a: Latency: time per request. Throughput: requests handled per unit time.

cards.q: What does 'four nines' of availability allow per year?
cards.a: 99.99% allows about 52 minutes of downtime a year.

children.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
children.summary: Rough QPS, storage and bandwidth math to size a system before designing it.
children.hook: Napkin math: right order of magnitude beats a precise wrong design.

cards.q: Estimate QPS for 100M daily active users making 10 requests each.
cards.a: 1B requests/day ÷ ~100K s ≈ 10K QPS average; plan for 2–3× peak.

cards.q: Roughly how many seconds are in a day?
cards.a: 86,400, round to ~100K for napkin math.

children.title: CAP & PACELC
children.summary: Under a partition you pick consistency or availability; otherwise latency vs consistency.
children.hook: When the phone line between offices is cut, either stop answering or risk giving stale answers.

cards.q: State CAP in one sentence.
cards.a: During a network partition, a distributed system must choose consistency or availability.

cards.q: What does PACELC add?
cards.a: Even without a partition, you trade latency against consistency (Else: Latency vs Consistency).

children.title: Consistency Models
children.summary: Strong, eventual, read-your-writes, causal: what readers are guaranteed to see.
children.hook: How fresh is the gossip you hear: instantly, eventually, or at least your own news?

cards.q: Give an example where eventual consistency is fine.
cards.a: Like counts or a social feed: a few seconds stale doesn't matter.

cards.q: What is read-your-writes?
cards.a: After you write something, your own reads always see it, even if others don't yet.

children.title: Scaling
children.summary: Growing capacity by adding machines and spreading load across them.
children.hook: Bigger truck vs more trucks.

cards.q: Vertical vs horizontal scaling: tradeoffs?
cards.a: Vertical is simple but capped and a single point of failure; horizontal scales out but adds coordination.

cards.q: Why should app servers be stateless?
cards.a: So any server can handle any request: you can add, remove or replace them freely behind a load balancer.

children.title: Load Balancing
children.summary: Spread requests across servers with round robin, least connections or hashing, at L4 or L7.
children.hook: A host seating diners evenly across waiters.

cards.q: L4 vs L7 load balancer?
cards.a: L4 routes by IP/port (fast, blind to content); L7 reads HTTP and can route by path, header or cookie.

cards.q: How do health checks work?
cards.a: The balancer pings each server periodically and stops sending traffic to ones that fail.

children.title: Caching
children.summary: Keep hot data in memory: cache-aside, write-through, write-back, with TTLs and eviction.
children.hook: Keep the stuff you use most on your desk instead of walking to the archive.

cards.q: Explain cache-aside.
cards.a: App checks cache; on miss, reads DB, writes the result to cache, returns it.

cards.q: What is a cache stampede and one fix?
cards.a: A hot key expires and many requests hit the DB at once; fix with request coalescing, locks or staggered TTLs.

children.title: CDNs
children.summary: Serve static and cacheable content from edge locations close to users.
children.hook: Warehouses near customers instead of shipping everything from one factory.

cards.q: Push vs pull CDN?
cards.a: Push: you upload content to the CDN. Pull: the CDN fetches from origin on first request and caches it.

cards.q: How do you invalidate CDN content?
cards.a: Versioned file names (cache busting), purge APIs, or short TTLs.

children.title: Rate Limiting
children.summary: Protect services with token bucket, leaky bucket or sliding-window limits.
children.hook: A bouncer with a ticket roll: tickets refill at a steady rate, no ticket no entry.

cards.q: Explain the token bucket algorithm.
cards.a: A bucket refills tokens at a fixed rate up to a cap; each request takes one; empty bucket means reject. Allows short bursts.

cards.q: Where would you enforce rate limits?
cards.a: At the API gateway or edge, keyed by user, API key or IP, often backed by Redis.

children.title: Data Storage
children.summary: Picking and scaling the right database for the access pattern.
children.hook: Choose the database by how you'll ask questions of it, not by fashion.

cards.q: SQL vs NoSQL: when to choose each?
cards.a: SQL for relations, transactions and ad-hoc queries; NoSQL for huge scale, flexible schemas or simple key access.

cards.q: What access pattern questions drive a storage choice?
cards.a: Read vs write heavy, query shape (key lookup, range, joins, search), consistency needs, size and growth.

children.title: SQL vs NoSQL
children.summary: Relational with ACID and joins vs key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores.
children.hook: A spreadsheet with strict columns vs a set of labeled boxes you can stuff anything into.

cards.q: Name the four NoSQL families with an example of each.
cards.a: Key-value (Redis), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j).

cards.q: What does ACID stand for?
cards.a: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

children.title: Indexes
children.summary: B-trees and LSM trees trade write cost for fast reads.
children.hook: The index at the back of a book: fast lookups, but every new page means updating it.

cards.q: Why do indexes slow down writes?
cards.a: Each write must update every index too.

cards.q: B-tree vs LSM tree?
cards.a: B-trees update in place and read fast; LSM trees append and compact later, so writes are faster.

children.title: Replication
children.summary: Copies of data for availability and read scale: leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless.
children.hook: Photocopies in several offices: safer and more readers, but copies can lag.

cards.q: What is replication lag and one problem it causes?
cards.a: Followers trail the leader; a user may not see their own just-written data when reading from a follower.

cards.q: How do quorums work (R + W > N)?
cards.a: With N replicas, writes go to W and reads to R; if R + W > N the sets overlap, so a read sees the latest write.

children.title: Sharding
children.summary: Split data across nodes by key range or hash; consistent hashing eases rebalancing.
children.hook: Splitting the phone book into volumes A–F, G–M, and so on.

cards.q: Range vs hash sharding?
cards.a: Range keeps neighbors together (good for scans, risk of hotspots); hash spreads evenly but breaks range queries.

cards.q: What problem does consistent hashing solve?
cards.a: Adding or removing a node only moves a small fraction of keys instead of reshuffling everything.

cards.q: What is a hot shard?
cards.a: One shard gets far more traffic than others, e.g. a celebrity's data.

children.title: Async & Messaging
children.summary: Decoupling services with queues, logs and events.
children.hook: A ticket counter: drop off your order, go do other things, pick it up later.

cards.q: Why put a queue between two services?
cards.a: To decouple them, absorb spikes, and keep working when the consumer is slow or down.

cards.q: Queue vs pub/sub?
cards.a: A queue gives each message to one consumer; pub/sub delivers each message to every subscriber.

children.title: Message Queues
children.summary: Buffer work between producers and consumers; at-least-once delivery and retries.
children.hook: A to-do pile between two coworkers who work at different speeds.

cards.q: What is a dead-letter queue?
cards.a: Where messages go after failing too many times, so they can be inspected instead of blocking the queue.

cards.q: Why must consumers be idempotent?
cards.a: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen; processing twice must not cause double effects.

children.title: Event Streams
children.summary: Append-only partitioned logs like Kafka that many consumers replay.
children.hook: A ship's log: append-only, and anyone can reread from any page.

cards.q: How does Kafka keep ordering?
cards.a: Ordering is guaranteed within a partition; messages with the same key go to the same partition.

cards.q: What is a consumer group?
cards.a: A set of consumers sharing a topic, each partition read by exactly one member.

children.title: Idempotency & Exactly-Once
children.summary: Make retries safe with idempotency keys and deduplication.
children.hook: Pressing the elevator button twice still calls one elevator.

cards.q: How does an idempotency key work for payments?
cards.a: The client sends a unique key; the server stores the result per key and returns it for repeats instead of charging again.

cards.q: Why is true exactly-once delivery hard?
cards.a: Networks can lose acks, so senders must retry; you get at-least-once plus dedup instead.

children.title: Reliability
children.summary: Keeping systems up and understandable when parts fail.
children.hook: Assume everything breaks; design so nobody notices.

cards.q: What is a single point of failure?
cards.a: A component whose failure takes the whole system down.

cards.q: Define SLI, SLO and SLA.
cards.a: SLI: what you measure. SLO: the target. SLA: the contractual promise with penalties.

children.title: Redundancy & Failover
children.summary: Replicas across zones and regions, with active-active or active-passive failover.
children.hook: A spare tire you've actually tested.

cards.q: Active-active vs active-passive?
cards.a: Active-active: all sites serve traffic. Active-passive: a standby takes over on failure.

cards.q: What is split-brain?
cards.a: Both sides of a partition think they're the leader and accept conflicting writes.

children.title: Timeouts, Retries, Breakers
children.summary: Bound waits, retry with backoff and jitter, trip circuit breakers to stop cascades.
children.hook: Don't keep redialing a dead phone; wait longer each time, and give up after a while.

cards.q: Why add jitter to retries?
cards.a: So many clients don't retry in sync and stampede the recovering service.

cards.q: What does a circuit breaker do in each state?
cards.a: Closed: requests flow. Open: fail fast. Half-open: let a few through to test recovery.

children.title: Observability
children.summary: Metrics, logs and traces to see what a distributed system is doing.
children.hook: Dashboard gauges, a diary and a GPS trail for every request.

cards.q: Metrics vs logs vs traces?
cards.a: Metrics: aggregated numbers over time. Logs: discrete events. Traces: one request's path across services.

cards.q: What are the four golden signals?
cards.a: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation.

children.title: Classic Designs
children.summary: Applying the building blocks to well-known interview systems.
children.hook: Same Lego bricks, different buildings.

cards.q: Walk through the steps you use for any design question.
cards.a: Requirements → estimates → API → data model → high-level design → deep dive on bottlenecks → tradeoffs.

cards.q: What do you trade off first when traffic 10x's?
cards.a: Usually strict consistency and freshness first, leaning on caches, async work and eventual consistency.

children.title: URL Shortener
children.summary: ID generation, base62 encoding, a heavy read cache and redirects.
children.hook: A coat check: hand over a long coat, get a tiny ticket.

cards.q: How do you generate unique short codes?
cards.a: Counter or ID generator (e.g. Snowflake) encoded in base62, or hashing with collision checks.

cards.q: 301 vs 302 redirect here?
cards.a: 301 is cached by browsers (less load, no analytics); 302 hits you every time (analytics).

children.title: News Feed
children.summary: Fan-out on write vs on read, with hybrid handling for celebrities.
children.hook: Deliver the newspaper to every doorstep vs everyone fetching it from the stand.

cards.q: Fan-out on write vs read?
cards.a: Write: push posts into followers' feeds at post time (fast reads). Read: assemble the feed at request time (cheap writes).

cards.q: How do you handle a user with 50M followers?
cards.a: Don't fan out their posts; merge them in at read time (hybrid).

children.title: Chat System
children.summary: WebSockets, presence, message ordering and storage for 1:1 and group chat.
children.hook: An open phone line instead of repeatedly asking 'any messages?'

cards.q: Why WebSockets over polling?
cards.a: A persistent two-way connection lets the server push instantly, without polling overhead.

cards.q: How do you order messages in a group?
cards.a: A per-conversation sequence number assigned by the server (or by the partition that owns the chat).
